                                        PROJECT NO. 58481
 RULEMAKING TO ESTABLISH                         §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD FORECASTING                          §
 CRITERIA UNDER PURA §37.0561                    §                     OF TEXAS

       TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS’ PROPOSED COMMENTS
           TO PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.194

                                   I.       INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) is comprised of a diverse group of business
sectors with industrial facilities in Texas, including oil and gas, air separators, steel mills,
petrochemicals, semiconductor fabricators, and others. TIEC shares the goal of establishing a
clear, uniform interconnection process and financial obligations for large load customers. If the
transmission system is built out for load that does not materialize, TIEC members (who are
predominantly large, high load-factor electricity users) will pay a substantial portion of any
underutilized investments.

       TIEC recognizes that the recent “race to market” in the hyperscaler/computing/artificial
intelligence (AI) sector is driving unrealistic load forecasts that need to be rationalized through
additional financial commitments and the demonstration of project viability/maturity. This was
the core goal of Senate Bill (SB) 6. At the same time, the Commission must not impose onerous
financial requirements that will deter ongoing economic development from the traditional
industrial community. Many of these traditional industries are struggling today under global
economic uncertainty. Many are also developing facilities that are a high priority for the state, and
even the nation, including some that received significant economic development incentives to
bring their operations to Texas. These companies are very cost-sensitive and risk averse, and the
Commission should be mindful that overly burdensome, inflexible requirements aimed at deterring
speculation in the AI/hyperscaler sector could materially chill growth from these businesses. The
final rules must balance the need to “legitimize” interconnection requests against the potential
unintended consequences for traditional businesses.

       TIEC appreciates Commission Staff’s (Staff’s) and the Commission’s efforts to
incorporate stakeholder feedback. However, TIEC respectfully submits that further refinement is
needed for the rule to be workable for traditional industry. In particular, TIEC is concerned that
the substantial, cumulative, and largely non-refundable financial commitments may freeze out

                                                 1
 traditional industrial growth without improving forecasting practices for this new type of large
load, which is proving to be less cost sensitive. The PFP currently requires (i) an Intermediate
Agreement with an Interconnection Study Fee of not less than $100,000 or $300,000, depending
on the load size, a $50,000 per MW financial security, and additional financial security for
significant equipment or services; and (ii) an Interconnection Agreement with financial security
for significant equipment or services and system upgrades, a non-refundable contribution in aid of
construction (CIAC) for direct interconnection costs, and a non-refundable Interconnection Fee of
$50,000 per MW. Notably, only 20% of the security amounts are actually refundable if an
interconnecting customer withdraws its interconnection request. The purpose of the financial
obligations established in this rule should be (a) to demonstrate financial viability and (b) as a
project progresses, to protect utilities and their customers against stranded utility investments.
Accordingly, these financial obligations should be right-sized to the actual risks and costs, and
fully refundable after covering those costs. If some of these provisions are instead aimed at
ensuring these new large loads contribute a certain amount to ongoing system costs, that is better
addressed in Project No. 58484, including consideration of TIEC’s minimum transmission charge
proposal. This will achieve the same outcome without unduly chilling legitimate growth from
traditional industry.

       The rigid capacity clawback provisions are even more problematic for large industrial
users. Under the PFP, if a customer fails to achieve a ramp milestone by six months, the large load
will be removed from the interconnection process and lose 80% of its financial security in addition
to the proposed non-refundable CIAC payment and $50,000/MW Interconnection Fee. For
industrial companies with long-term expansion plans entailing tens of billions in capital
investment, changes are almost inevitable. Construction may be delayed for any number of
reasons outside of a customer’s control. Phases of a project may be accelerated, delayed, or
canceled as market conditions evolve over time. This is the reality of the global economy and
large, complex projects. Requiring a large industrial project to completely forfeit capacity
earmarked for a planned expansion because a milestone is missed by six months is not
commercially workable.

       As detailed below, TIEC seeks modifications to the rule in the following areas, in order of
priority to traditional industrial companies.


                                                2
 1. Remove or substantially revise the six-month capacity clawback requirement. The
   Commission should remove the PFP language that requires ERCOT to re-allocate a large
   load’s interconnection capacity if it fails to meet an energization milestone by six months.
   This does not reflect the realities of executing on a complex, capital-intensive industrial
   project. At a minimum, the time period should be extended from six months to a year, and
   there should be a Commission-led process for obtaining a good cause exception should the
   timeline need to be adjusted further.
2. Remove the Interconnection Fee and make the CIAC refundable, less actual utility
   costs. The PFP creates two completely non-refundable payments that are not tied to actual
   cost exposure for the utility or other customers: (1) a non-refundable $50,000/MW
   Interconnection Fee due at the time an Interconnection Agreement is executed, and (2) a
   non-refundable CIAC. The Interconnection Fee is not tied to any actual cost or potential
   for stranded costs, and a non-refundable CIAC does not make sense when the utility may
   not have incurred any costs. Both charges should be cost-based and refundable after
   covering any actual utility costs associated with a canceled project. To the extent the
   Commission is concerned that new large load customers will not appropriately contribute
   to ongoing system costs, the Commission should address those concerns in the cost-
   allocation and ratemaking mechanisms under consideration in Project No. 58484, including
   consideration of TIEC’s minimum transmission rate proposal.
3. Reduce or bifurcate the generic $/MW Intermediate Agreement security. The
   Commission should also reduce the generic financial security amount in the Intermediate
   Agreement because it only needs to be substantial enough to help determine whether a load
   is “real.” A security amount of $20,000/MW would meet this objective. If, however, the
   Commission is concerned that it is not substantial enough for all large loads, it could adopt
   a tiered $/MW security amount based on load size. For an incremental increase in
   requested peak demand between 75 MW and 249 MW, the security could be $20,000/MW,
   while a large load customer with an incremental increase in requested peak demand that is
   equal to or greater than 250 MW would be required to pay $50,000/MW. This would match
   the bifurcation of the Interconnection Study Fee and would impose less burden on
   traditional industrial growth.
4. Financial security requirements under the Intermediate Agreement should not be
   cumulative. Any financial security provided for significant equipment or services in the
   Intermediate Agreement should be applied to reduce the $50,000/MW flat security
   requirement. The $/MW security under the Intermediate Agreement is not based on any
   actual costs of serving the large load, it is meant as a proxy. If some costs are known at
   the time of the Intermediate Agreement, financial security for those costs should count
   against the “proxy” security requirement.
5. Release Intermediate Agreement Security upon signing an Interconnection
   Agreement. Several provisions of the rule require the utility to draw on the security
   provided under the Intermediate Agreement for various costs, when a customer moving
   past the study phase may prefer to pay cash or post a different form of security. All excess
   security under the Intermediate Agreement should be released when the customer posts
   security under a final Interconnection Agreement or, at the customer’s election, applied to
   the Interconnection Agreement security requirements. An interconnecting large load


                                             3
    should retain the option to post a different type of security under the Interconnection
   Agreement, which will be in place for a longer period of time.
6. Extend the deadline to sign an Interconnection Agreement and implement a Standard
   Large Load Interconnection Agreement (SLLIA). Large businesses will have difficulty
   negotiating final Interconnection Agreements and securing financial security of this
   magnitude in only 30 days, as required by the PFP. Under Planning Guide Revision
   Request (PGRR 115), for example, customers were given 180 days. Ideally, TIEC
   recommends that the Commission adopt an SLLIA to simplify these negotiations, which
   could allow a shorter commitment period (perhaps 45 days). However, until that is in
   place, the Commission should extend the deadline to 60 days following the completion of
   the interconnection study to give customers a realistic opportunity to receive and analyze
   the study results, initiate and complete internal approval processes, finalize capital
   allocation decisions in the context of competing projects and sites, negotiate the
   Interconnection Agreement, and execute the Interconnection Agreement with the required
   financial commitments.
7. Refund any outstanding financial security less actual costs if a load withdraws or
   reduces its interconnection request. Any financial security provided under the
   Intermediate or Interconnection Agreement should be fully refundable to large load
   customers, less any actual costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting
   TSP if a load cancels, withdraws, or reduces its interconnection request. A tiered refund
   structure will naturally occur based on costs incurred during the period of time the project
   remains in the interconnection process. The longer a large load project remains in the
   interconnection queue, the more actual costs the utility will have incurred. As noted
   previously, to the extent the Commission is concerned that new large load customers
   should lose their security amounts to contribute to ongoing system costs, the Commission
   should address that concern in the cost-allocation and ratemaking mechanisms under
   consideration in Project No. 58484. As noted above, this refund approach should also
   apply to CIAC.
8. Clarify that “Batch Zero” Base Load is not required to conform an existing
   interconnection agreement. The Commission should clarify that large load customers
   that have previously been studied and have existing, signed interconnection agreements are
   in an advance stage of development, and should not be subject to new financial
   requirements established in this rulemaking. Requiring these loads to satisfy the full suite
   of Project No. 58481 requirements would impose redundant burdens on customers with
   sites under development, conflict with SB 6, and potentially shift capacity from customers
   that have been in the queue for years to newer market entrants.
9. Allow options to satisfy the Interconnection Agreement’s site control requirements.
   A legally binding option to purchase or lease property should qualify as site control at both
   stages of the interconnection process, consistent with the framework that has been
   successfully applied to generation interconnection requests. Many projects cannot get
   funding to execute a lease until they can demonstrate an interconnection, particularly those
   relying on project financing.
10. The threshold for determining the Interconnection Study Fee should be based on the
    incremental increase in peak demand. As drafted, the size of the Interconnection Study

                                             4
         Fee is based on the “requested peak demand” of the large load customer, instead of the
        load’s incremental increase in peak demand. This should be clarified to avoid penalizing
        existing large sites pursuing only a modest expansion.
     11. Expand the entities that can provide a guaranty. The current language, if strictly
         construed, would prevent all entities other than corporations from providing guaranties,
         even if they meet the required credit rating (e.g., among others, partnerships, limited
         partnerships, limited liability companies, joint stock companies, and trusts). While
         guaranties from other entities may be less common, large load customers should have the
         option of obtaining a guaranty from any legal entity, as long as the entity meets the
         Standard & Poor’s or Moody’s credit requirements.


                                     II.       COMMENTS

A.      The capacity clawback provision should be removed or substantially revised to reflect
        commercial realities.

        TIEC has serious concerns with the proposed mandatory capacity reallocation provisions
in proposed §25.194(h), which require an interconnecting DSP or TSP to notify ERCOT and
initiate financial security drawdown when a large load customer fails to satisfy a ramp milestone
by only six months. The consequences of missing a milestone by six months are severe: (i) the
interconnecting DSP or TSP must draw down on the large load customer’s financial security, apply
it to outstanding amounts owed, refund only 20% of the remaining balance to the customer, and
remit the remaining 80% to the interconnecting TSP for application as an offset to rate base; and
(ii) ERCOT must reallocate the non-utilized capacity to other customers.

        It is extremely common (perhaps more common than not) for massive, large-scale
industrial complexes to experience delays for a variety of reasons. This could include supply chain
issues, labor shortages, geopolitical conditions, permitting delays, litigation, and many other
scenarios. Typically, complex industrial facilities also plan for multiple phases over a longer term
period, which could be five to ten years following expected energization. This requires predictions
about economic and commercial conditions far into the future that may change substantially over
time and impact project scope and timing. At the same time, these are often facilities that are high
priorities not only for Texas but for the nation. For example, many of these projects receive
substantial economic development packages to entice them to site in Texas or in the U.S.

        Requiring these sites to automatically forfeit their capacity and lose hefty security postings
if a ramp milestone is missed by six months is simply not workable. TIEC is not aware of any


                                                  5
 other state with a similar requirement, and this could drive major, strategic projects out of Texas.
At a minimum, this time period should be extended to a year, and there should be a Commission-
led process for obtaining a good cause exception if the timeline will slip further than a year. TIEC
does not have specific language at this time but strongly recommends additional work on this
concept among Commission Staff and stakeholders before a final rule is adopted.

B.     The non-refundable Interconnection Fees should be removed, and CIACs should be
       refundable less any actual utility costs.

       The Proposal for Publication includes two non-refundable fees that are not cost-based.
First, a large load customer must pay a non-refundable Interconnection Fee of $50,000 per MW of
contracted peak demand. This fee is not based on the facility’s actual interconnection costs.
Instead, it is to be applied to the interconnecting TSP’s rate base. 1 As TIEC has emphasized
throughout this rulemaking process, the goal of the financial security requirements under SB 6 is
to protect other customers against stranded costs or cost-shifting—not to require large load
customers to write upfront checks for more than their fair share of grid costs. When a large
customer executes an interconnection agreement, the customer must provide substantial financial
commitments, including a non-refundable Interconnection Study Fee of $100,000 or more, a
$50,000/MW financial security under the Intermediate Agreement (as proposed), financial security
for significant equipment and services based on the utility’s estimated costs, a CIAC covering all
direct interconnection costs, and additional financial security for system upgrades. Layering a
non-refundable $50,000/MW Interconnection Fee on top of these existing obligations is
duplicative and not tethered to actual cost exposure for the utility or its other customers.

       Similarly, making the CIAC non-refundable and requiring full payment at the time of the
Interconnection Agreement does not track any actual cost exposure. The changes to the rule
eliminating standard cost allowances mean CIAC payments will be even more significant than
they are today. CIAC payments are to cover direct interconnection costs for a customer. In
TIEC’s experience, CIACs can range from a few million dollars to $30 million, $50 million, or
more depending on the customer’s service specifications. However, depending on when a
customer withdraws a project, the utility may have actually spent $0 on these facilities. Requiring
a customer to completely forfeit their entire CIAC is unjustified if there are no actual costs to


       1
           PFP § 25.194(f)(7).

                                                  6
 cover. A non-refundable CIAC is particularly punitive when combined with the Interconnection
Fee discussed above. These two features will require businesses seeking to site in Texas to make
massive, non-refundable cash outlays before their projects are earning any revenue.

       As TIEC has noted in prior comments, standardized fees under SB 6 should generally
reflect the actual costs that a utility bears to support a customer’s interconnection at each stage of
a project’s development, and excessive fees should not be used as a development deterrent. At
this stage of the interconnection process, the interconnecting utility and ERCOT have completed
their studies, so actual interconnection costs can be reasonably estimated. The customer’s CIAC,
financial security for significant equipment and services, and financial security for system
upgrades are calibrated to recover any actual costs the large load could impose on the system. A
generic, non-refundable fee bears no relationship to the utility’s actual expenditures and provides
no targeted protection against stranded costs, but it will be a significant economic development
deterrent.

       Importantly, SB 6 also envisions the various methods of demonstrating financial
commitment as a menu of options—not as cumulative layers of cost that must be independently
maintained. Once a more precise cost estimate is provided under an Interconnection Agreement,
a customer should be permitted to continue by securing project-specific cost exposure, not paying
additional arbitrary charges. As TIEC has consistently maintained, once a utility and its ratepayers
(including TIEC members) are protected from the expected costs of any build-out, additional
financial obligations will only deter business development by tying up cash or credit in the utility
planning process. This is particularly harmful for cost-sensitive traditional industrial companies
that may be pursuing multiple new sites each year and for whom excessive financial commitments
can impede expansions in Texas. For these reasons, the Commission should reject the proposed
$50,000/MW non-refundable Interconnection Fee and the non-refundable CIAC, and instead rely
on refundable, cost-based financial security mechanisms.

       As discussed in more detail below, to the extent the Commission is concerned that new
large load customers will not appropriately contribute to ongoing system costs, the Commission
should address those concerns through the cost allocation and ratemaking mechanisms under




                                                  7
 consideration in Project No. 58484, including TIEC’s “minimum transmission charge” proposal.

C.       The generic security in the Intermediate Agreement should be reduced to
         $20,000/MW or bifurcated.

         TIEC appreciates that the Commission reduced the generic financial security requirement
from the $100,000/MW level recommended in the initial discussion draft to $50,000/MW. That
reduction reflects a meaningful step toward calibrating this requirement to its intended purpose.
However, TIEC respectfully submits that $50,000/MW remains substantially higher than
necessary to accomplish the Commission’s legitimate objectives and urges the Commission to
reduce the generic financial security amount to $20,000/MW of incremental increase in requested
peak demand.

         The dollar per MW security is meant to “screen out” requests that do not have the financial
wherewithal to actually execute on a large, capital-intensive project. As such, it should act as a
proxy for the eventual security requirements under an Interconnection Agreement, and not just a
high hurdle to deter interconnection requests—particularly from legitimate, traditional businesses
exploring expansion opportunities in Texas. The security amount only needs to be substantial
enough to demonstrate viability, but not so costly that it is a deterrent to economic activity.

         Traditional industrial operations compete in global markets and are extremely cost
sensitive. As discussed in the Senate Business & Commerce Committee meeting on April 1, 2026,
both the Commission and Legislature share the concern that traditional manufacturing will get
caught up in the interconnection application process, which will lead to the loss of traditional
businesses that want to move to or expand in Texas. 2 An upfront financial commitment of the
magnitude contemplated by the proposed rule may deter legitimate and desirable industrial activity
from locating or expanding in Texas, undermining the very business development the Legislature
sought to promote when enacting PURA § 37.0561. 3 Traditional manufacturing should not be

         If the Commission is hesitant to reduce the security obligations for all large loads, the
Commission could consider adopting a bifurcated $/MW security amount based on load size,
similar to the distinction for the large load Interconnection Study Fee. For example, a large load
customer with an incremental increase in requested peak demand that is equal to 75 MW and less
than 250 MW would be subject to a $20,000/MW security requirement, while a large load
customer with an incremental increase in requested peak demand that is equal to or greater than
250 MW would be required to pay $50,000/MW. Both tiers provide sufficient security to ensure
that the load is legitimate and committed. This approach also ensures that the security requirement
is proportionate to the scale of the interconnection request, promoting fairness and still protecting
ratepayers and system reliability. Further, this approach would minimize the significant financial
impact on traditional industrial consumers because most of their interconnection requests are
below the 250 MW threshold.

D.     Security for significant equipment or services under the Intermediate Agreement
       should apply as an offset to the $/MW security requirements.

       As currently drafted, the PFP could require a large load to provide both a generic dollar
per MW security under the Intermediate Agreement and additional financial security for
significant equipment or services. The financial security for significant equipment or services is
needed to protect ratepayers from the risk that a large load cancels its interconnection request after
the interconnecting utility purchases long-lead time equipment needed to serve the large load. For
example, auto transformers, transmission breaker bays, and other long-lead time equipment must
be ordered well in advance and are known to be necessary.

       However, it does not make sense for these security amounts to be cumulative. Especially
at this early stage of the interconnection process, loads should not have to provide an excessive
amount of financial security. As explained previously, the only purpose of the generic dollar per
MW security is to determine whether a load is “real” and could actually execute on a project.
Providing an equal or greater amount of security for long-lead time equipment still ensures the
load has “skin in the game.” The dollar per MW security is a proxy; it is not based on the actual
costs of serving the large load. When some costs of serving the load are actually known and can
be individually secured, this should reduce the “proxy” security under the rule. For example, if
the security for long-lead time equipment is greater than the generic security, the large load should
not be required to post additional security. Alternatively, if the long-lead time equipment is less
than the generic security, the customer would post the difference between the actual cost of the
long lead-time equipment and $50K/MW (or $20K/MW if TIEC’s position is incorporated).

§25.194(d)(10).

               subsection is due at the time that the intermediate agreement is executed. A large
               load customer must post financial security with the interconnecting DSP or the
               interconnecting TSP [in the amount of $50,000 per MW of the requested peak
               demand for new interconnection requests or of the incremental increase in the peak

                 demand for expanded interconnection requests] 5. The financial security amount(s)
                shall be reduced by the amount of security provided for significant equipment or
                services procured prior to executing an interconnection agreement.

E.      The PFP should specify that all security amounts under the Intermediate Agreement
        will be released once the Interconnection Agreement is signed.

        Currently, the Proposal for Publication requires the financial security under the
Intermediate Agreement to be applied directly to the financial obligations under the
Interconnection Agreement, rather than released or refunded. Specifically, §25.194(f)(7)(A) and
§25.194(f)(8)(B) require the utility to draw down on any unused financial security provided from
the Intermediate Agreement and to apply it to the non-refundable Interconnection Fee and the
financial security for significant equipment or services. Instead of requiring the security to be
applied to the financial obligations under the Interconnection Agreement, the final rule should give
interconnecting entities that are moving forward to the next step additional optionality. An
interconnecting large load may prefer to directly pay the Interconnection Fee (if retained in the
final rule) with another source of funding, rather than allowing the utility to draw down on a letter
of credit or corporate/parental guaranty, which can be a very involved process with additional
transaction costs. Similarly, a large load may prefer to use a different form of security to meet the
Interconnection Agreement’s financial security for significant equipment or services under
§25.194(f)(8)(B). There is no reason to force a large load to use the same sources of funding for
the Interconnection Agreement. To protect other ratepayers, the Commission could wait to release
security under the Intermediate Agreement until the customer posts replacement security under
the Interconnection Agreement, which should include allowing an election to carry forward
security under the Intermediate Agreement if the customer chooses.

        The construct for automatically carrying forward security in the PFP also fails to account
for any new cost information following completion of ERCOT’s interconnection studies. Notably,
the language under the PFP is unworkable if ERCOT’s studies result in lower interconnection costs
than initially assumed. Security requirements based on the expected costs of the required system
upgrades are typically tens of millions of dollars for transmission-connected loads. However, with

       Additionally, the rule fails to adjust the lower financial obligation if ERCOT does not
approve the full energization request of the large load. Currently, ERCOT’s Batch Study Process

capacity. Loads could be subject to a reduced interconnection capacity for six years, if not longer.
Loads subject to allocation should not be forced to maintain security for the entire interconnection
request if they are not receiving service for a significant amount of time. This could result in a
reduction to the security amounts provided under the Intermediate Agreement and the
Interconnection Agreement.

F.     The 30-day commitment period to sign an Interconnection Agreement should be
       extended to 60 days, and the Commission should ultimately implement a Standard
       Large Load Interconnection Agreement (SLLIA).

       Traditional industrial customers cannot realistically negotiate and post security under a
final Interconnection Agreement in 30 days, as proposed by the PFP. Notably, ERCOT has
forklifted this requirement into Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145, which provides
that if a load has not executed an Interconnection Agreement and provided the required security


                                                12
 within thirty days of receiving study outcomes from a Batch Study, the load will not be able to
continue in the interconnection process and will have to wait until the next Batch Study cycle,
essentially losing its place in the interconnection queue.

       This timing is not workable for most traditional industrial consumers and is much more
stringent than the 180-day requirement in PGRR115. Today, signing a final Interconnection
Agreement and posting financial security typically takes several months. Companies typically
require formal board or executive committee approval before committing capital at this scale, and
the internal governance processes necessary to obtain such approval frequently take longer than
30 days on their own. Further, interconnecting loads usually go through multiple rounds of
negotiations before finalizing the language for an agreement. A 30-day timeline is further
complicated by the reality that many traditional industrial facilities are simultaneously evaluating
multiple projects and sites inside and outside of Texas. Internal capital allocation decisions are
competitive, iterative, and subject to intense internal review.

       The rule, as proposed, would effectively require large industrial customers to obtain pre-
approval of all financial commitments and to begin negotiating the Interconnection Agreement

        commercial realities.

         TIEC respectfully submits that further refinement is needed for the rule to be workable for
traditional industry. These companies are very cost-sensitive and risk averse, and the Commission
should be mindful that overly burdensome, inflexible requirements aimed at deterring speculation
in the AI/hyperscaler sector could materially chill growth from these businesses. Specifically,
TIEC seeks the following modifications to the rule, in order of priority:

•    Remove the six-month clawback requirement because it does not reflect the realities of
     executing on complex, capital-intensive industrial proj ects. At a minimum, the time period
     should be at least a year with a process for obtaining a Commission-led good cause exception.
•    Remove the Interconnection Fee and make the CIAC refundable, less actual utility costs. The
     Interconnection Fee is not tied to any actual cost or potential for stranded costs, and a non-
     refundable CIAC does not make sense when the utility may not have incurred any costs. Both
     charges should be cost-based and refundable after covering any actual utility costs associated
     with a canceled proj ect.
•    Bifurcate the generic $/MW Intermediate Agreement security or reduce it to $20,000/MW
     because it only needs to be substantial enough to help determine whether a load is "real."
•    Make the Intermediate Agreement security requirements non-cumulative to avoid
     unnecessarily tying up cash and credit. Any financial security provided for significant
     equipment or services should reduce the proxy $/MW security requirement.
•    Release Intermediate Agreement security amounts when the Interconnection Agreement is
     signed, or, at the customer' s election, apply the fees to the Interconnection Agreement
     requirements, less actual utility costs.
•    Extend the deadline to sign an Interconnection Agreement to 60 days to match the practical
     realities of executing an Interconnection Agreement. The Commission should also adopt a
     Standard Large Load Interconnection Agreement to simplify negotiations.

•    Refund all financial security amounts, less actual utility costs if a customer changes or
     withdraws its interconnection request to protect ratepayers without penalizing businesses.
•    Exempt previously studied loads with executed interconnection agreements from being
     required to conform their agreements to the new requirements of this rule.
•    Make other practical changes to the rule, including recognizing purchase or lease options as
     valid site control, calculating the Interconnection Study Fees based on incremental load
     growth, and allowing guaranties from any creditworthy entity to qualify as acceptable security.
